description:
Dalmahoy stands in parkland between Kirknewton and Ratho, a short distance west of Edinburgh, and it occupies a genuinely distinct place among the properties in this collection: unlike the Scots Baronial turrets and castellated silhouettes that define most of Scotland's castle-hotels, Dalmahoy is a classical Palladian country house, completed in 1725 to a design by William Adam, one of the most influential Scottish architects of the early 18th century and patriarch of the remarkable Adam family of architects that would go on to shape Georgian Britain. The house was built for George Dalrymple, a younger son of the Earl of Stair, and was originally known by the more romantic name 'Belvedere' before later taking the name of the surrounding estate.

Ownership passed to the Douglas family in 1760, and the connection has proved genuinely enduring: the estate remains in the hands of a direct descendant of that same family, the 22nd Earl of Morton, to this day — a continuity of ownership spanning more than two and a half centuries. Dalmahoy's history also carries a specific, evocative connection to Mary, Queen of Scots, who is said to have visited the house. Following her celebrated escape from imprisonment at Loch Leven Castle — an escape aided by the Douglas family, whose members controlled the castle at the time — the keys used to lock the gates were thrown into the loch to prevent pursuit. Those keys were later recovered and, remarkably, are preserved today at Dalmahoy, a tangible physical link between the estate and one of the most dramatic episodes in Mary's turbulent reign.

Dalmahoy's transformation into a hospitality venue began relatively recently in the context of its own long history: the estate opened as a Country Club in 1976, initially offering just 10 rooms. The scale of the operation has grown enormously since then, and Dalmahoy today operates as a substantial 215-room hotel, with two restaurants and bars, a spa featuring an indoor swimming pool, and — its most distinctive feature — two full 18-hole golf courses laid out across 1,000 acres of parkland, with views extending to Edinburgh Castle and the bridges spanning the Firth of Forth.

Those two golf courses represent Dalmahoy's clearest and most significant point of public, non-resident access. The Championship East Course, designed by the celebrated golf architect James Braid to a demanding standard exceeding 7,400 yards from the championship tees, and the more flexible West Course — which can be played as a full 18 holes or shortened to 9 or 13 for visitors with less time — are both open to advance bookings from members of the public who are not staying at the hotel, confirmed both through Dalmahoy's own official booking channels and multiple third-party golf booking platforms. This mirrors the pattern already established elsewhere in this collection at Dalmunzie Castle, where a hotel's golf course similarly functions as a genuine, confirmed point of non-resident access distinct from the accommodation itself.

Given its combination of genuine 18th-century architectural pedigree, a documented connection to Mary, Queen of Scots, and two publicly bookable championship-standard golf courses within easy reach of Edinburgh, Dalmahoy offers a meaningfully different profile from the Baronial castle-hotels that make up most of this pilot collection — a reminder that Scotland's grand historic country houses come in more than one architectural tradition.

William Adam's legacy at Dalmahoy also places the house within a genuinely significant chapter of British architectural history: Adam went on to father Robert and James Adam, whose neoclassical work would later define Georgian architecture and interior design across Britain and beyond. Dalmahoy stands as one of the earlier, formative works in that family tradition, built while William Adam was still establishing the Palladian idiom in Scotland that his sons would later refine and popularise on an even grander scale.

faqs.question: Can non-residents play golf at Dalmahoy?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both of Dalmahoy's 18-hole golf courses — the Championship East Course, designed by James Braid, and the more flexible West Course — are open to advance bookings from members of the public who are not staying at the hotel, confirmed through the hotel's own official booking channels and multiple third-party golf platforms.

faqs.question: Why is Dalmahoy classified as a palace rather than a castle on this site?
faqs.answer: Dalmahoy is a classical Palladian country house, completed in 1725 to a design by William Adam, without the turrets, battlements or castellated silhouette that define the Scots Baronial 'castle' style seen at most other properties in this collection. Its architectural character places it closer to Scotland's palace and grand country-house tradition, the same reasoning applied to Atholl Palace elsewhere on this site.

faqs.question: What is Dalmahoy's connection to Mary, Queen of Scots?
faqs.answer: Mary, Queen of Scots is said to have visited Dalmahoy, and the estate holds a striking physical relic connected to her: the keys of Loch Leven Castle, thrown into the loch during her famous escape from imprisonment there in 1568 — an escape aided by the Douglas family, who controlled the castle. Those keys were later recovered and are preserved today at Dalmahoy, which has been owned by descendants of the same Douglas family since 1760.
